The third review, against head 8f7cf3f, found ten issues. Most of the earlier ones are fixed, and what's left is mostly edge cases and readers that haven't been moved over yet. Like the earlier rounds, it traced the code only and ran nothing. I fetched the PR head and checked by hand the earlier findings that this round didn't re-raise.

*Fixed since earlier rounds*

• *-e -m, --amend --no-edit and -C* (round 2, #3 and #5): prepare now works out whether git opened an editor from GIT_EDITOR=:..
• *commit.cleanup=strip with -m "#…"* (round 1, #8): it now handles each cleanup mode explicitly..
• *The review re-run guard* (round 2, #2): head_checkpoint_flags.go:55 now uses CommitCheckpoint, the same resolver attach uses..
• *The confusing --generate error* (round 2, #9): it now names the checkpoint that sits outside the final block..
• *Test isolation* (round 2, #8): attach_test.go:1991 now calls IsolateGitConfigEnv..
• *Repeated git config lookups* (round 2, #7): the result is now cached per hook with sync.Once, which brings its own risk (new #8)..
• *Strict trailer-block check* (round 1, #5): mixed blocks with Signed-off-by or (cherry picked from commit …) lines are now accepted..
• *core.commentChar=auto* (round 1 #3 / round 2 #4): this is now deliberate. Post-commit reads with #, the same way git interpret-trailers does. If git itself doesn't see the trailer, Entire doesn't either..

*Partly fixed*

• *Explain views reading a different ID* (round 2, #1): the main explain view now reads the last ID of the final block, but the branch listing and --checkpoint search still read the first (new #5)..
• *Typing next to the trailer in the editor* (round 1, #2): post-commit now accepts a stamped trailer the user moved, but attach and explain don't (new #2)..

*New findings*

1. *An appended trailer can unlink a commit* (cmd/entire/cli/trailers/trailers.go:438).

• *Mechanism:* appendTrailerLine only joins a final paragraph made purely of trailers. The readers also accept mixed blocks and skip comment lines..
• *Effect:* the OPF rewrite (manual_commit_opf_rewrite.go:575) can add Entire-OPF-Applied: true as a new paragraph. That paragraph becomes the final block and pushes the existing Entire-Checkpoint trailer out of it. Attach then treats the commit as unlinked and rewrites it again..
• *Fix:* make the appender use the same block rules as FinalCheckpointTrailers..

2. *Post-commit and the readers disagree on a moved trailer* (manual_commit_provenance.go:258). When the user types body text below the trailer, post-commit still condenses into X. Attach sees no final-block trailer and adds a second one (Y). explain --generate refuses the commit, and a later amend doesn't keep X. The PR's doc admits this one.

3. *A commented-out trailer still counts* (manual_commit_provenance.go:258). The moved-trailer fallback uses the unanchored ParseAllCheckpoints regex. Under a cleanup mode that keeps comments, a user who unlinks the commit by writing # Entire-Checkpoint: X still gets the session condensed into X.

4. *Squash and redo inheritance still scan the whole message* (manual_commit_hooks.go:727, manual_commit_redo.go:132). After git merge --squash and an editor commit, the squashed commits' trailers are indented in the body. They count as already present, so nothing goes into the final block. With no new session content, the squash commit ends up with no final-block link. Documented as a limitation.

5. *Some explain paths still read the first ID* (explain.go:1713, 1731, 2471). The branch listing and the --checkpoint commit search still use ParseCheckpoint. On a squash commit with [X inherited, Y stamped], entire explain <sha> shows Y, the branch listing shows X, and explain --checkpoint Y finds no commit. The comment at checkpoint_api_reader.go:371 is now out of date. Documented as a limitation.

6. *A user-exported GIT_EDITOR=: brings back the trailer-only commit.* Editor detection treats it as "no editor", so a message saved untouched is recorded as just Entire-Checkpoint: X. With -v, the trailer goes below the diff and git discards it. Documented as a limitation.

7. *The prompt leaks into history under commit.cleanup=whitespace* (manual_commit_hooks.go:611). The explanation comment, including # Last Prompt: <user prompt>, is still written when git keeps comment lines. git then records it in the commit permanently. I'd rank this highest of the undocumented ones, because it puts prompt text into git history.

8. *A cached error can disable a whole hook* (hooks.go:72, manual_commit_hooks.go:3061). GetGitDir and gitCommentConfig cache their result for the rest of the hook using whichever ctx calls first. If that first call runs under a cancelled or expired budget ctx, the error is cached. Every later marker read and write then silently returns nothing.

9. *The trailer regex misses Key : value* (trailers.go:410). git allows whitespace before the colon, so a block like Reviewed-by : Bob plus Entire-Checkpoint: X is rejected, and prepare stamps a duplicate trailer.

10. *Extra hook latency* (manual_commit_provenance.go:233). recordStampedTrailer opens the repo again and re-resolves the parent commits, and commit-msg now runs a git config on every linked commit.

*Not re-checked:* GitHub squash-merge bodies (round 1, #6), where every squashed commit's trailer ends up in the final block, are likely still affected; this round didn't raise them and I didn't check. The hard-wrap note (round 1, #10) I'm dropping, because sessions-and-checkpoints.md itself is wrapped at 80 columns and the new text matches it.

I'd fix #7 and #8 before merging; neither is documented and both can silently go wrong. #1 is the same "use one block rule everywhere" problem as before, now on the write side. #2 to #6 are limitations the author has documented, so whether to accept them is a call for you or the author.

89af8a14e fix(trailers): place and read the trailer as git records it
Only the final trailer block links a commit, so each git commit mode
that left Entire's trailer elsewhere lost its link. Prepare and
commit-msg guessed what git already knows, and some readers kept the old
rule:

- Git runs its commit hooks with GIT_EDITOR=: when it opens no editor
  (githooks(5)). Both hooks now read that instead of the source word or
  the message's last line: a -m, --amend --no-edit or -C message gets
  its trailer appended with its own lines in place, a -m -e one gets it
  above git's comment block, and commit-msg judges an emptied message by
  git's cleanup.

# General Review Lessons

- Make a guard's zero-match check count only the matches it is meant to protect. Matches that are always present, like the guard's own allowed cases, keep the check from ever firing.
- Test a guard by planting a violation and by breaking its detection, and see it fail both times. A guard that passes on clean code proves nothing.
- Before acting on a review finding, check whether existing tests or contracts explain the current shape. A structural test can be why the code looks the way it does.
- When code reads a user-owned config into a typed struct and writes it back, keep the fields it does not model. Any new reason to rewrite the file otherwise silently deletes user data.
- Make a new outer timeout longer than every internal budget on that path. Otherwise the kill fires before the code's own graceful fallback.
- Before setting an explicit timeout, look up the platform's current default for that exact event; an explicit value can shorten the budget rather than add one.
- When splitting known from unknown JSON keys to preserve them, decode only the exact known keys and keep every other key, case variants included, as unknown. `encoding/json` matches field names case-insensitively, so decoding the whole object lets a key like `"Command"` overwrite the real field.
- When a change makes a fix command riskier, changes which command to run, or adds a new place that reports an existing failure, check every place that already reports it (status, doctor, enable, help text) so they all give the same fix. Otherwise one screen sends people to the safe fix and the next to the destructive one, or one command prints the same failure twice with different fixes.
- When a test plants a failure to cover an error branch, make sure an earlier step doesn't fail first; otherwise the assertion passes without ever running that branch.
- Select an agent's final report by a marker it carries (such as the contract line), not by its position in the event stream; a trailing tool call or an empty message ID moves a position-based boundary.
- When code keeps state so a later run can retry, test the retry itself. A test that checks the kept state against the same expression the code uses would pass even if that expression were wrong.
- When decoding user-editable JSON into maps or pointers, skip null elements before writing to them; `[null]` decodes to a nil map and a write panics.
- Review a PR that is behind main against current main, not its own base: build both and run the same repro. Its tests pass on its old base even when keeping its side of a conflict would undo a fix merged since.
- When wiring user config into a new path, test it with a broken config too. A user rule that silently fails to load leaks the same way as one that was never wired.
- Make a fail-closed check fire only on the failure it guards against, not on a whole class of errors. A refusal on any settings error blocks unrelated cases and pushes users toward a less safe escape hatch, such as an unredacted `--raw` bundle.
- Read the Trail's current description and resolved findings before drafting review comments. The trail description can be newer than the PR description and may already list known follow-ups, which turns "you missed this" into a question about scale or timing.
- When a PR claims corpus validation, check what the corpus contained, and test on inputs from outside it, such as other languages and other codebases. A corpus drawn from one codebase can pass while common idioms elsewhere break.
- When a PR adds a second implementation of an existing contract, such as another way to compute an offset or boundary, check it uses the same rule as the existing path and test it with input that hits the contract's edge case. A mock that maps input one-to-one passes whichever rule is used.
- Don't rewrite a value before other detectors scan it; collect detections on the unchanged value and merge them. Masking first can break anchored or overlapping matches and expose text the old pipeline redacted.
# cli Review Lessons

- When replacing a git subprocess with a filesystem parser, check that it still works in bare repos and still respects exported `GIT_DIR`/`GIT_WORK_TREE`; git handles cases a parser misses.

**#1 Writer block rule.** The mismatch is real, but the effect the review describes can't happen. The OPF rewrite only touches `entire/checkpoints/v1` commits. Their messages (`buildCommitMessage`, `persistent.go:1285`) never carry `Entire-Checkpoint`, and attach reads user commits, not those. On user commits the mismatch never unlinks anything either, because a new trailer paragraph is always a valid final block. What it does do: it pushes the user's own trailers out of git's final block when that block is mixed, such as `Signed-off-by:` plus a note line. Git then stops reading them as trailers.
- **Fix:** `appendTrailerLine` joins any block that `isTrailerBlock(lines, "")` accepts. That is the strictest reading, so the OPF reader and post-commit both accept the result.
- Comment lines still count as non-trailer lines when writing, because different readers skip different prefixes.
- `countTrailerBlock` goes back into `isTrailerBlock`, since its second caller disappears.
- One test row's expected output changes to joined: "trailing hash line starts a new block".

**#2, #3 and #10's marker cost (moved trailer).** The root cause is the stamp marker added in 89af8a14e. It lets post-commit link a commit by a rule that attach and explain can't apply. Its whole-message check also matches `# Entire-Checkpoint: X`.
- **Option A (recommended):** remove the fallback and the marker: `stampedTrailerFile`, `record/clear/takeStampedTrailer`, and 8 call sites. Then one rule applies everywhere: if git's final block doesn't name the checkpoint, the commit isn't linked. The session's work rolls into the next linked commit, or `entire attach` links it.

  - The cost: a body typed below the trailer leaves the commit unlinked again (the round 1 #2 case), but consistently across all readers.
  - `TestTrailerAuthority_BodyTypedBelowTheTrailerStillLinks` flips to assert every reader sees the commit as unlinked.
- **Option B:** keep the fallback, but only accept a whole, uncommented trailer line. This fixes #3; #2 and the marker cost stay documented.

The squash commit keeps git's indented copy in the body and gains the ID in its final block. `TestPrepareCommitMsg_SquashDefaultMessageKeepsInheritedTrailerOnce` changes from "exactly one `Entire-Checkpoint:` line" to "the final block names it once". I'd add a matching redo test.

**#5 Explain paths.**
- `--checkpoint` search matches any ID the commit names, so Y finds the squash commit and X still finds it too.
- The branch listing uses `CommitCheckpoint`, the same as `explain <sha>`.
- So the listing doesn't run `git config` once per commit, I'd export the existing per-operation snapshot (`withCommentConfig` becomes `WithCommentConfig`) and wrap the walk in it.
- I'd also fix the stale comment at `checkpoint_api_reader.go:371`.

**#6 User-exported `GIT_EDITOR=:`.** No code change. Git sets `:` for hooks only when it opens no editor, and a `:` the user exported reaches the hooks unchanged, so the two look identical. The only other signal is git's status block. That block is missing under `commit.status=false`, and a `-m` message ending in a `#` paragraph would look edited. - `gitCommentConfig` caches only a read made while its ctx was still live, using a mutex instead of `sync.Once`.

**#9 Trailer regex.** I checked with git 2.50 `interpret-trailers --parse`. Git accepts `Reviewed-by : Bob`, `Key<tab>: v`, `1abc: x` and `-x: y` as trailers, and rejects `Key x: y`. - `Entire-Checkpoint : X`.

For each fix, I'd write the failing test first, then the code, with one commit per finding group. I'd run `mise run check` before committing, and nothing gets pushed without your approval.
